title: Peak pressures climbing
objective: Measure intra-abdominal pressure in at-risk patients because examination cannot detect abdominal compartment syndrome, and recognize its effects on kidneys, lungs and heart

brief.situation: 10:00 in a surgical ICU. You are Mr. Abara's nurse. He is 63, the day after repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, intubated and sedated. He received about 11 L of fluid and blood in the first 24 hours.
handover: Over the last two hours: peak airway pressure up from 28 to 38 cm H2O, urine output down to 10 mL/h, MAP drifting down, heart rate up.
The resident felt his abdomen at 08:00: 'distended but soft enough'. An intra-abdominal pressure order exists 'every 4 hours'; none has been done since surgery.
Unit policy: bladder pressure supine, at end-expiration, zeroed at the mid-axillary line, with no more than 25 mL instilled; report any value over 20 mmHg to the surgeon at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: What and how
parts.criteria: Abdominal compartment syndrome after massive resuscitation: IAP over 20 measured correctly (supine, end-expiration, mid-axillary zero, 25 mL) with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, rising peak pressures, falling MAP); examination cannot detect it.
parts.modelAnswer: After 11 liters his bladder pressure, measured properly, is over 20, and his kidneys, lungs and heart are all failing together. That's abdominal compartment syndrome. Feeling his belly can't tell you that; you have to measure.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Tells the surgeon now for decompression; NG to suction; neuromuscular blockade as ordered; no further fluid bolus; measures by protocol, not head-up or with a large volume.
parts.modelAnswer: Tell the surgeon now for decompression, put the NG to suction and give the ordered blocker while we wait. No more boluses, they'd raise the pressure. And measure it the right way: flat, end-expiration, 25 mL.

scoring.modelReasoning: After 11 L of resuscitation, falling urine output, rising peak airway pressures and a falling MAP together point to the abdomen. Examination cannot detect abdominal compartment syndrome, so measure the bladder pressure by protocol: supine, at end-expiration, zeroed at the mid-axillary line, with no more than 25 mL instilled. A pressure over 20 with new organ dysfunction is ACS: the kidneys are compressed, the diaphragm is pushed up and venous return falls. Tell the surgeon now for decompressive laparotomy, put the NG tube to suction and give the ordered neuromuscular blocker meanwhile, and give no more fluid boluses.

defQ.ask: While you measure: what defines abdominal compartment syndrome?

choices.label: IAP over 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction

defQ.explain: IAH is a sustained IAP above 12; ACS is an IAP over 20 with organ dysfunction or failure. Distension is not a sensitive or specific finding.
